narrative.title: Why pharma, why now
narrative.body:
I spent the first part of my career in institutional finance, most recently at Goldman Sachs, managing 20+ institutional relationships across multi-million dollar syndicated loan portfolios. The real skill there wasn't the numbers. It was earning the trust of time-strapped people who had every other option available to them, reading what each one actually needed, and knowing dense, jargon-heavy contracts well enough to solve real problems with them. In 2023, I stepped back to raise my two kids.

In 2025, I watched a stranger save someone's life during a medical emergency, and it pushed me to earn my EMT license. I finished in the top 5% of my cohort at UT Dallas. During clinicals I worked in the emergency department, on patient transfers, and in the ambulance, including administering medication under protocol, and completed training in pharmacology fundamentals. What stayed with me was how often a patient's outcome traced back to whether the right medication had reached them, and whether the provider treating them had the right information at the right moment. That's the part of the chain a rep owns.

I've always been achievement-oriented and tenacious, and pharmaceutical sales is where those instincts and this clinical foundation actually converge. I know what I don't have: two years with a B2B outside sales title on my resume. What I do have is the underlying work that requirement screens for. As a full-time volunteer representative across Nebraska, Iowa, and South Dakota, I ran a three-state territory for 18 months with my own CRM pipeline, daily pre-call planning, post-call evaluations, and hard weekly targets. I built that territory from underperforming to one of the strongest in the region, and I did it by developing the community gatekeepers who could open doors a cold pitch never would. That is territory building, gatekeeper access, and rejection tolerance, learned the hard way rather than in a training program.

I also bring two things most candidates coming out of a traditional B2B seat don't. I'm clinically fluent, so I can hold a real conversation with a physician and their staff on day one rather than spending six months learning to. And I'm bilingual in Spanish, which across DFW physician offices means I can build genuine rapport with front office staff and gatekeepers, the people who decide whether you get five minutes or none.

I live in the DFW metro, my kids are in preschool with full-time childcare in place, and I'm looking for a territory where I can bring my hunger and grit. My approach is simple: know the product, know the territory, build real trusting relationships with the people in it, and keep pivoting until I find the right need and the right angle to close.

startStories.title: Sales Performance & Hitting the Number
startStories.teaser: Setting the targets, then hitting them, under real pressure.
startStories.body:
At Vivint, I wasn't in the field, I was setting the targets the field reps had to hit. I built the executive forecasting models and diagnosed the performance gaps that became the strategic goals for the team, then presented a business case to senior leadership that secured a $2M+ revenue expansion opportunity. That's the metric-setting side of a sales number: understanding where it should come from before anyone chases it.

At Goldman Sachs, hitting the number meant something more literal. I completed 10 to 20 complex transactions a week with zero-defect accuracy, in a 70+ hour workweek with no room for error. That's the discipline of consistently meeting hard output targets under real pressure, the same discipline it takes to hit a quota month after month.

startStories.title: Pre-Call Planning & Post-Call Evaluation
startStories.teaser: How I built a call planning discipline from scratch in a three-state territory.
startStories.body:
As a volunteer representative across Nebraska, Iowa, and South Dakota, I built this process from scratch. Before every visit, I wrote a specific pre-call plan objective. After every visit, I ran a post-call evaluation, tracked through a CRM pipeline, capturing the objections and concerns I heard so I could handle them better next time. That discipline turned an underperforming territory into one of the strongest territories in the region.

At Goldman Sachs, the same instinct showed up differently. When a senior client pushed back on a contract term, I found the misread myself, got internal leadership aligned, and closed the objection out before it became a lost account. Prepare for the objection, then close with a clear next step, works the same whether the stakes are a contract or a prescribing decision.

startStories.title: Trusted Relationships & Win-Win Agreements
startStories.teaser: What I learned from the one gatekeeper everyone said not to bother with.
startStories.body:
The clearest example of this is a community leader I worked with as a volunteer representative, the gatekeeper to an entire network of prospects. He hadn't worked with a single missionary in years, and everyone before me said not to bother. Instead of pushing him directly, I built a relationship with his wife over weekly lunches until I learned he missed playing soccer with a group he'd lost touch with. I organized a recurring soccer event and told him all he had to do was show up. He did, and over time he went from ignoring us completely to mobilizing his own network on our behalf, and eventually inviting us to celebrate the Fourth of July with his family, something no missionary before me had ever been invited to. Resistance is usually just information about what someone actually values.

At Goldman Sachs, I managed 20+ institutional relationships with senior decision makers who had every option available to them and no obligation to stay loyal. Relationship-first account management, reading what each one needed and delivering it, is what kept them.

startStories.title: Call Planning & Territory Coverage
startStories.teaser: Deciding who gets called on, how often, and why.
startStories.body:
Across a 3-state mission territory, I built a repeatable cadence of visits and referrals instead of relying on cold outreach, the same coverage-and-frequency thinking a call plan requires.

At 1-800 Contacts, I built a nationwide marketing heat map across 42,000+ U.S. ZIP codes to identify exactly where spend and coverage should be concentrated for maximum reach, the analytical backbone of deciding who gets called on, and how often.

startStories.title: Market & Clinical Intelligence
startStories.teaser: Reading a territory with data, and reading a clinical room with training.
startStories.body:
At Vivint, I diagnosed territory-level performance gaps and built executive forecasting models in technical SQL, Snowflake, and Python to understand exactly where the market was moving and why.

At 1-800 Contacts, I didn't just build the market intelligence, I shared it. After building the ZIP code targeting framework, I personally trained the Analytic Team on how to use it, the same alignment this role asks for between field insight and the broader team.

And on the clinical side, my EMT training in the emergency department, on patient transfers, and in the ambulance, plus coursework in pharmacology fundamentals, is where my clinical and product fluency for physician office conversations starts.

startStories.title: Developing Advocates & Referral Networks
startStories.teaser: Finding the person whose voice already carries weight, and earning it on their terms.
startStories.body:
During my 18 months as a Spanish-speaking volunteer representative, each area had an appointed community leader who was essentially the gateway between local members and our work. Without his engagement, we were cut off from the exact network our prospects needed to join. Mine hadn't worked with a single missionary in years, and everyone who came before me said not to even bother.

So instead of pushing him directly, I built a relationship with his wife first: weekly lunches, genuine friendship, listening for anything that told me who he actually was. She eventually mentioned he missed playing soccer with a group, so I organized a community soccer event and told him all he had to do was show up. He came, and we made it recurring. Over time he went from ignoring us completely to making referrals and mobilizing his entire network, and he eventually invited us to celebrate the Fourth of July with his whole family, something every missionary before me had called unimaginable. That's the motion this work takes: find the person whose voice already carries weight, develop them on their own terms, and let their credibility open doors a cold pitch never could.

At Goldman Sachs, I served as the face of the firm's brand to senior financial decision-makers, executing white-glove standards specifically to differentiate a company's value proposition from competitors, the brand-differentiation half of the same skill.

I provided direct patient care in the ED, on patient transfers, and in the ambulance, including administering medication under protocol, and completed training in pharmacology fundamentals, the exact clinical fluency and patient-centered focus a pharma rep needs. Assisting an ER physician during a high-acuity emergency tracheotomy, and supporting emergency air transport intake from rooftop helipad arrival through trauma bay admission, taught me to stay calm and execute under real pressure while working alongside physicians, nurses, EMTs, firefighters, and trauma teams, the same matrix-environment collaboration a pharma rep needs across a prescriber's care team.

Getting fluent in dense, legal-jargon-filled contracts well enough to solve real problems with them is the same skill it takes to get fluent in dense clinical and scientific language fast: mechanism of action, payer language, competitive data, and making it land for the person across the desk.

Many of the children I advocated for were navigating serious medical and behavioral needs, which gave me an early, first-hand understanding of what's at stake when care doesn't reach someone. Building trusted relationships with judges, attorneys, families, and multidisciplinary stakeholders through emotionally intelligent communication is the same patient-centered, matrix-environment stakeholder management a rep needs to operate credibly across a prescriber's full care team.

I went in with classroom Spanish and came out fluent, using it every day for 18 months with hundreds of families and individuals across Nebraska, Iowa, and South Dakota, proof I can pick up a new language, technical or otherwise, and actually put it to work in the field. Creating pre-call plan objectives and executing post-call evaluations, tracked through a CRM pipeline, is the same call planning discipline this role requires to optimize coverage and frequency to key customers, and onboarding and mentoring a new representative while consistently hitting daily and weekly targets is the coachability hiring managers look for in a rep who can build referral-driven access from scratch.
